title: Ike Robinson's banjo lessons and joining Jelly Roll Morton's band
summary: Ike Robinson coaches Levy on banjo. Morton then calls him for a banjo job and he plays with the band in Chicago, about 1927.

story.theme_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section: instruments and players
story.community_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section's changing role

blocks.x: I was with Wickliffe and Tressie and Ike, they got a picture they're gonna give me of who I looked when I was young. And I will. You two fellas been together a long time then. Oh, I know Nike. Well, I tell you, when the times started changing and the banjos got so popular, I went and got a banjo. And by knowing harmony and I knew the piano pretty good, and I stayed home for four solid months with that banjo. And so a fellow told me, says, you play good, but you're playing too straight. He says, why don't you go see Ike and let him give you some pointers. Let him show you a thing, because Ike's really got something on that banjo. I said, man, he makes it tall. So I did. I got Ike and I said, Ike, can you come over and help me out. So Ike came, he said, now play me so and so. He had his banjo and he played the chords and played rhythm, played everything. And I was just in thought with his playing. So I said, what's the first thing I want to do? He says, well the first thing, and he hit a kind of, what was it, a triplet roll or something, Ike, and da da da, and he put some syncopated strokes, and he says, now when you play, he said, don't play too many bars the same. See, he said, sound the same. And he says, then variate your chords, don't play that same chord too long, two, three measures, the same position of the chord, like a B flat chord with D top, switch around and play it. And he said, now watch. And he started the singing and he'd play the banjo and he'd run up and down his hand and down, he'd change the inversion of the chord, that's what he really was, inversion of the chord, and then at the same time he put a little, a little rhythm lick in there, see? Syncopation. Yeah, a little syncopation, a little rhythmic lick, and he stayed up there, oh, he stayed up there, the first time he came, stayed about two hours with me. And he gave me, he gave me quite a lift, because I realized that I had the technique, my fingers were fast and I had the musical knowledge and I loved the banjo and I loved music. And so from then on it just seemed like I, Ike was so busy, I was making records and he was playing with different bands and everything. And so, but that really gave me an incentive to do more and it gave me a lift, because I was just hitting straight chords and mostly keeping time from then on. Then I got, I got pretty good. So, I was sitting home one day practicing and the phone rang, it was down in the union, and General Martin was on the phone. And I said, General, I said, how are you? I said, I haven't seen you since, that was about 19, well I said, I haven't seen you in three or four years. I said, remember I was down in your booking office, I was trying to get a band together, and I said, you had a booking office, and he said, yeah, but listen, I want to talk to you right fast. He says, I need a banjo player, I said, can you cut the stuff? I said, I can. He says, well then tell me you can, and he says, come on down to rehearsal, he said, because I got some engagements to play, and he said, I'll talk to you. So I was really thrilled to play with the great Jell-O-Robos. So I went down. Was that the MCA digs? I think so. I came down, they were rehearsed down the union, no, down the local 208. So I came down to rehearsal and they had about seven pieces of music. All the rest was there. So, but he said sit right by me now and watch my right hand. And so I did. Went through the rehearsal and I was surprised at myself because I did so good. Of course I was kind of inspired too, and then I had practiced the chords, oh I knew every chord all up and down the banjo. And I did the woodshedding home. So he said, I'm satisfied. And what Ike had showed me, the licks, I put a few of them in, they gave me a couple of breaks, and gave me a couple of intros. And so I felt real happy about it. So we played the first engagement, so he asked me, did I want to go on the road, he's going to try to make it to New York. he was driving, he was a show from driving, because he was just trying to get, I think, trying to get back on his feet again. So we went and I played, and Walter Barnes, the little boy that got run up the fire, Walter Barnes, he wanted a young band, so he got Walter Barnes himself.
